newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks boosted by upbeat retail sales.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks boosted by upbeat retail sales.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks ended higher Thursday, buoyed by upbeat reports on retail sales for January, but the mood on Wall Street was cautious ahead of Friday's report on January jobs data.

The 30-stock Dow Jones industrial average closed up 26.16 points at 6,773.06. In the broader market, advances led declines 1,233 to 1,219 on active volume of 519 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Dow component Sears, Roebuck & Co. jumped 1-3/8 to 49-7/8 after reporting strong sales in January.

"Several retailing companies gave us better-than-expected numbers, and we got some good activity in the group for the first time in a long time," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
Analysts said apparel stores reported standout results, with chain stores such as Gap Inc. and Limited Inc. as well as key department stores posting strong numbers.
Gap shares rose 2-3/8 to 32-1/4, Limited gained 1/4 to 17-3/8, and Wal-Mart Stores Inc. rose 1/2 to 23-5/8.

The buying interest was clearly tempered, however, as investors warily awaited key employment and wage data due Friday morning before the stock market opens. Markets often respond violently to surprises in the report, which is considered a key leading indicator of inflation.
"I don't think anyone was going to take an extreme position going into tomorrow's numbers," Orlando said.
Analysts said any gain of more than 275,000 jobs in non-farm payrolls could trigger a sell-off in financial markets.
The concern is that with the jobless rate declining, there could be a buildup in inflationary pressures stemming from a tight labour market and stepped-up wage demands by workers.

Economists surveyed by Reuters expect the report to show the unemployment rate declined slightly in January to 5.2 percent from 5.3 percent in December, while average hourly wages are expected to show a modest 0.2 percent increase.
Technology stocks remained under pressure, as investors backed away from the top-tier names that led the most recent leg of the market's rally.
Intel Corp. fell 4-1/8 to 153-1/8, bringing losses on the high-flying shares to 11-5/8 points over the last two sessions. Microsoft Corp. sank 1-1/4 to 97-1/8.
"We saw a restless rotation in the market today and tech stocks lacked the sponsorship and the bounce they once had," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.

But the selling pressure clearly abated from Wednesday's intense level and analysts said several issues appeared to find support, such as Cisco Systems Inc., which gained 7/8 to 63-7/8 and Gateway 2000 Inc., up 1-3/4 to 57-1/4.
Almost forgotten by the end of the session was the highly awaited release early in the day of President Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget.
The budget blueprint was considered a test of credibility on the path to a balanced federal budget by 2002.
Stocks showed little response to the presentation, even though many Wall Street professionals criticised at the budget's assumptions.
Among individual issues, USA Detergents Inc. slid 13-7/8 to 20-3/8 after the company warned of weaker than expected fourth quarter earnings.
Manpower Inc. surged 5-3/8 to 35-3/8, after it reported higher fourth quarter earnings and said its European operations showed signs of recovering.
The Nasdaq composite index was off 2.04 points at 1,346.40.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 1.87 to 780.15. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.38 to 585.03.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.15 to 409.89. The average share was up 12 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,511.876 up 13.512 or 0.18 percent.
